Segotep is a 20+ year old company. Their 750W & 850W "GM" PSUs are rated "Tier B" at the PSU Cultists Network and "Gold Efficiency" & "A- Noise" at Cybenetics Labs. So, I think the manufacturer has reasonable credibility. I've not seen a better value on a 650W 80+ Gold PSU. As always, DO NOT TRUST USER REVIEWS FOR PSUs. The only way to get objective data on these things is from proper reviewers like Tom's Hardware or Gamers Nexus. Consult the Cultists Tier List Source Spreadsheet for more info, and do not make a purchase based on the subjective data in this review.
That said, this is a solid unit. True SFX, reliable, plenty of wattage*, gets the job done. Fully modular and the cables are nice.
However, it is not quiet, not loud enough to be annoying but audible over good quality CPU/GPU cooling at moderate loads. The advertised semi-passive operation up to 40% load is false; the fan kicks on with a vengeance around 175-200 W of full system draw. My particular example also came with the EPS connectors tangled through each other in a way that was impossible to separate.
*a design flaw causes the 850W version of this unit to get flaming hot at its full capacity. I would personally treat this unit as a 700 W since it has the same component choice.

name: Lian Li EDGE 1300 W 80+ Platinum Certified Fully Modular ATX Power Supply
comments: The edge PSU works perfectly with the King 95 Ultra case. I like how the cables are already braded so you don't have to get extension cables to make the build look good.

Pros:
Cables come braided and have combs on them
L shape design makes plugging in cables a breeze
Comes with a dedicated 12V 2x6 port and cable (the prongs that plug into the GPU and powersupply are bright blue so when you go to install it makes it easy to identify that the plug is all the way in)
Cables come in a nice bag that can be reused to keep spare cables in
The wattage options this power supply comes in
Adds 4 additional ports for USB 2.0 headers to plug into
Cons:
Availability (almost always out of stock)
Mainly designed for dual chamber cases (Ex. Lian Li O11 EVO XL)
Minor Grievances:
-None
Final Thoughts:
This is a very nice power supply from Lian Li. I would absolutely recommend this, only if you are building a PC in a dual chamber case (most cases coming out today are). The L shape makes installing and routing cables a breeze and makes cable management much easier. The cables you will normally see in the front of the PC (24 pin, 8 pin PCI-Es, and 12V 2x6) come braided and have combs on them to keep them organized. Comes with a dedicated 12V 2x6 port and cable, along with a two 8 pin PCI-Es to a 12V 2x6. My only issues is that these power supplies are almost always on back order and never in stock. I got lucky and grabbed mine from a restock on Amazon.

For the cases that can accommodate it, I think the RMx Shift series is a great innovation in consumer PC supplies.
Pros:
performance; Cybenetics-certified Gold Efficiency / A Noise rating
ATX 3.1-certified; includes 2x8-pin PCIe->12V-2x6 adapter.
side-facing cable inputs; facilitates far easier cable access and management compared to the standard PSU layout.
Corsair Type 5 micro-fit cables; notably more compact connectors than the Type 4 predecessor.
fluid dynamic bearing fan
100% Japanese 105 °C capacitors
10-year manufacturer’s warranty
Cons:
cost; way over-priced compared to similarly performant 850 W power supplies.
limited compatibility; incompatible with dual chamber fish tank-style cases, or any chassis narrower than 210 mm in width.
lack of native 12VHPWR / 12V-2x6 connector.

You can have 2 computers, 2 bluetooth devices, and an AUX device all playing audio through the headset at the same time with no issue. My setup is have it used with my computer, playing instant mic feedback, and connected to my phone if needed for a call, all playing at once.

Overall I really like this headset! I've used the Arctis line before and when I did I had one main issue. I would often start feeling pain in my head from wearing the headset too long, and because of that I was hesitant to get another Arctis headset. However having had some time with this new headset, I am very pleased to say that I have had 0 head pain (and minimal headphone hair). At times I even forget that they are on my head.

Let's start with the most important things. These are 250 ohm open back headphones. By design they won't block out noise and they need at least a moderately powerful amp to drive them. Try to use them in a loud room or drive them with a standard headphone jack from a phone, laptop, or even the front panel I/O of most desktop computers and you'll be disappointed.
Use them in a quiet room with an amp that has the power to drive them and they're incredible.
"Mount Beyer" is definitely present - the brightness associated with most Beyerdynamic headphones is absolutely a thing, but to my ears this is only a problem if you're using an equalizer or other processor (like Creative's SBX sound processor). Use one of these and the brightness is almost piercing and uncomfortable. HOWEVER, if you turn off the equalizers and sound processors and drive the headphones directly, with audio that has no "surround effect" or "audio enhancers" applied, these are easily among the best sounding headphones I've ever experienced.
I think that the problem with things like Creative's SBX or other audio processors designed to "enhance" sound is that they almost invariably boost the same rage where these headphones already have fantastic response. Just use a flat EQ with no additional processing and let the headphones do their thing. You'll be glad you did. The soundstage is expansive and everything comes through beautifully - the sound from these is wonderfully detailed and clear. Well worth the cost of entry.
As far as comfort and other matters, the large ear cups rest comfortably without crushing your ears and the open back means they breathe well so they don't get hot. Even with glasses they don't get uncomfortable even after a long listening session.

The 250ohm version of this really needs to be connected to an amp so I added a Schiit stack to my build. These headphones are wonderful. I came from a wireless SteelSeries Arctis 7 and I just couldn't stand the popping and random disconnects anymore. A friend talked me into going with a real audio solution instead of defaulting to "gaming supplies" and it was the best decision I ever made. The open back profile of this headset is extremely immersive and makes everything you're playing feel like open world. I use these as my daily drivers for everything but music.

comments:

I put off getting a proper headset for a long time because ones I had used before would always hurt my ears or feel like they were squeezing my head. The mic stick is detachable, and it is somewhat flexible allowing you to bend it to be closer to your mouth. I'm not super picky about sound quality but I can tell that the headset is a step up from my wireless earbuds, and it has just enough sound canceling to improve my gaming experience without making me completely deaf to what is going on around me.
If you want the two RGB areas to cycle through the rainbow while showing different colors like the headset does out of the box, you will need to set them to separate rates of change in G HUB, otherwise the color will sync. I personally do not notice the lights in my peripheral vision unless I turn off all the lights in the room besides my headset and monitor. I don't care much about the lights though, the reason I chose this headset was for comfort and the lights are just a bonus feature. I like that they turn red to indicate the battery is low, but you can also check the battery level by lightly tapping the power button.
It may be worth noting that my head is smaller than average, so folks with larger heads than mine might be less comfortable than I am. Also, I saw another review here where the person said they could hear the signal of the device communicating with their computer for RGB changes, but that has not been an issue for me and I have pretty sensitive hearing (I can hear high pitched noises from certain electronics that others can't hear) but it may be something to be mindful of if you are SUPER sensitive.

I had a SteelSeries Siberia 800. Used it for about 2 years. Problem was the rotating part of the left earcup broke, as it was only made out of plastic. Tried to fix it with superglue, didn't work. I hear loud static unless I fiddle with that broken part.
So I was looking for a new SteelSeries headset, but they're all sold out from the sellers I trust. Then I found out about the Corsair Virtuoso from Linus Tech Tips and Hardware Canucks.
Aluminum frame is pretty sturdy. But just like the Youtubers say, it's too tight. Then again, if my experience with my Siberia 800 were any indication, give it about 3 weeks at least, and the headband should loosen up.
The sound is alright, after tweaking the equalizer from Corsair iCUE software. Corsair's virtual surround sound is weird for music, but in games it did surprisingly well. I was playing Prey (2017) prior to getting these headphones, and now with them on, even if I can't see some flying robot, I could tell when it was flying above me. I could tell when it was closing in and when it was directly above my head. The sensation felt so real that the first time it happened, it made me instinctively duck my head a bit in real life.
If you play a lot of FPS games, consider checking out these headphones (or just headphones with virtual surround in general, if you don't like Corsair) as the ability to tell when a sound is above or below you helps a lot.
A few problems:
Mic may not work in wired mode if you connect the USB from a USB hub. Best to connect it directly to your PC's back/front USB port. This is a common problem with devices connected to a USB hub as the hub typically only has one USB port's worth of power, so it can't give enough juice if you connect too many power hungry devices.
Wireless signal interference can happen. I turned on my Joycons wirelessly and while it was pairing, the music I was listening to stuttered, and I hear a short crackling/static sound. Supposedly, Corsair's "Slipstream" wireless dongle automatically switches to a less used frequency to give it the best possible connection, so maybe it will take time for it to do so the more you turn on wireless devices in your room.
If you have near 100% RAM usage, it starts to stutter (then again, everything in your PC will slow down with 100% RAM usage).

name: Corsair HS80 RGB Headset
comments: Great sound and is super comfortable. Lights adjustable on the iCue app, if that's your thing. The microphone is crisp and haven't heard any complaints from my buddies. Was gifted from a coworker and a major upgrade from the Steel Series Arctic 3 wired I was using forever.

This headset seems to be fairly decent. I got these in March and updated them as soon as I got them with the iCUE software. The battery life is a little less than expected. As long as you remember to charge it after every couple of uses your golden. There is not an accurate battery level indicator to know what the charge is. The icon in iCUE is basically fully charged, half charged, and low battery. The range is not as far is indicated either. I get 15 feet away into my hallway in my single family home and it cuts out entirely. This is likely attributed to having the dongle plugged into the pc on the back of the PC instead of the single top port of the PC, and other wireless traffic in the area.
I got my wife the HS80 Max, which has almost triple the battery life, and can get to our back porch (about 50 feet through wood studs and drywall.
Overall a 4 out of 5. Battery and lower than expected range is my reason.
Very comfortable, although can have a little bit of squeezing

This headset is something I actually did consider returning. Right out of the box the sound is just awful. It's flat, tinny and just doesn't have any depth to it. I was further worried by this still being the case when turning on Dolby Atmos. I do think that the Corsair Void headsets have better surround sound quality overall, but after some major tweaking of EQ's and getting used to a different sounding pair of headphones, I did finally find a spot where I am happy with them. The major reason I kept on to these is that they are not as high profile as the Void series and the mic quality is actually pretty nuts for a gaming headset. You'd be forgiven for mistaking it for a standalone mic with how good it sounds. The wireless part is new to me and I really appreciate the freedom it gives, the lack of wire is worth paying for if you're not a complete sound buff who needs something like a studio headset. The distance on these things isn't great but it reaches 90% of our small rented space, I lose connection when I am at the edge of the kitchen and in the downstairs bathroom, so not awful. I do see this being a bigger issue in a full sized house. The wireless charge with lights on lasts me about 18 hours so I tend to have them on charge before they run out. Though I do take care not to leave them charging overnight as to avoid damaging the battery life.
Overall probably not the best option out there, but certainly not the worst and I am finding myself becoming happier with them the longer I use them.
Edit: So it is currently June 6th 2023 and I bought these on November 28th 2022. The earpads have already fallen apart, I've requested some more via the 2 year warranty but this really brings the rating down to a 3 star. The build quality of the cups is appalling for the price.

It's very comfortable and light, good swivel, enough headband adjustment, etc. The biggest problem for some people would be it's open back so if you live in a loud house or in a big city with trains and **** (or a loud keyboard) it could be a problem. name: SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless for Xbox X|S, and Xbox One Headset

specs.Model: Arctis Nova Pro Wireless for Xbox X|S, and Xbox One

comments:
Pros: Great headset, chat mix is useful, Sonar has built-in streamer mixing. I get compliments on my mic quality. The hot-swappable batteries might make the headset worth buying for that alone. In general, the hardware is top tier (with the exception of the ear cups).
Cons: Sonar/SteelSeries GG has to be running for the headset to work properly, and I swear it resets my settings every few days. It's maddening. The app has good features, but once I set things up I don't want to have to think about your stupid app and/or change my settings back every time I want to use the headset. Stop shuffling my device switching settings. Stop crashing when I use my KVM switch and killing the sound to my desktop. SteelSeries, for the love of god fix your app, or make it optional. There's a whole DAC sitting on my desk doing nothing that could be doing a lot of this stuff without forcing me to interact with your software.
Also, the noise-canceling is mid, and I eventually had to switch out the earcups for Wicked Cushions because the stock ones were getting pretty uncomfortable. Unfortunately, I think this did change the sound profile a bit.
A little tight on the head, but SteelSeries does it again.

specs.Features:
Top-of-the-range open, dynamic hi-fi stereo headphones
Systems with narrow tolerances (+/- 1 dB), hand-picked in pairs
High-quality titanium/silver finish

comments:
Comfortable, build well, and last long. Intimate staging but endgame tonality and timbre. HD580, 600 and 650 blow any other dynamic open back out of the water, except maybe stuff like ZMF and maybe the Auroris Borealis.
Definitely way better than treble death headphones like dt770/990/1990/1770. those are very yucky.

It's easy to decide with its balanced and detailed soundscape if you want more treble/bass/etc, and to upgrade to according intermediate open-back pairs like the Sundaras or Beyerdynamic DT-990/1990 pros. For me, though, the balance was just perfect, and I don't plan on changing these out for many years. Just get an amp along with them. I went with the FiiO K7. These are also still mindblowing how good they are to me, as I went from a Razer Kraken headset to these lol. I used to like those things but they sound like absolute crap now.

The unit worked well... for a week. After that, I was getting F01/F02 errors every other time I tried to turn my computer on. Restarting the unit would work... for about a day before the errors would come up again. After three times, I gave up: since F02s indicate actual physically blown fuses, and since I'm working near potentially-flammable items and carpet, I decided it wasn't worth the risk and refunded the unit. The repeated start-stops when the unit fuses blew probably damaged my computer's components far more than had I just been using the wall outlet... Maybe I just got unlucky, but given this is my first experience with APC, I was extremely disappointed. I'll just be using a standard surge protector from now on.

I have my modem/router, pc, and monitor all plugged into the battery side, and this is one of the few times that I've been happy I didn't spend extra for a more powerful unit.

A fantastic choice of UPS! It's a Line Interactive type, which means that it will power your PC off of mains power directly, avoiding the battery altogether unless there is a blackout or brownout, and it compensates for inconsistent mains power by automatically correcting undervoltages or overvoltages. It also has something called "Pure Sine Wave" technology, which is just a fancy way of saying that it's digital DC-to-AC transformer is good enough to fool a high-end "Active PFC" PC power supply into thinking it's getting "authentic" AC.
Runs out of the box, but also includes a USB hookup and pleasant monitoring software (that stays quiet when you aren't looking for it) if you want to monitor your UPS more directly. The monitoring software cheekily integrates with both Ubuntu and Windows 10, providing battery charge levels to the OS as if the whole computer were a laptop!
Buy one if you're considering one and you won't regret the purchase.

comments:
It gets the job done. In Australia, CyberPower units are usually the cheapest for around $250-$400 AUD for 1000-1300VA units.
However, there was a video circulating on Reddit of a unit catching fire if you unplug and re-plug it into the wall during use. It was blamed on some QA issues with some flammable glue(??). I have emailed CyberPower for comment and they have said that it is due to improper grounding. You are not supposed to unplug it from the wall, even when the wall switch is off (and therefore, ungrounding the unit) and plug it back in (reintroducing the ground connection) as it can catch fire. Scary. A reminder to never mess around with these things otherwise they will explode in your face. Only unplug UPSs while the unit itself is switched off.
Mine hasn't caught fire yet, so, 5 stars for now!

name: M-Audio BX5 D2 140 W Speakers
comments:
I bought this pair of speakers back in 2015, and they have been wonderful ever since. I went with M-Audio because I had just gotten an M-Audio midi controller shortly before these speakers and was impressed by the quality of the product. Doing some research led me to these, and they've never really disappointed me.
Letting them run for a few hours will inevitably make them warm up, but they never get HOT. I've left these things on overnight multiple times, and I always cringe at wasting power and possibly running the lifespan of the speakers down. But even after hours of running, they still stay a very reasonable temperature, and don't develop any noticeable problems with audio fidelity.
When I was on older laptops & desktops, I would get a speaker buzz due to ground loop. I think this is less the fault of the speakers themselves, and more a result of the power supply of the computer or laptop (i.e. not the PSU, but the actual circuit you're plugging into at the wall), and the unique audio hardware of each different computer. Your mileage may vary, but I had used a "Ebtech Hum X Voltage Hum Filter" from Amazon, and it cured all my ground loop buzz problems with these speakers and my set up in general.
Little blue LEDs are located between the tweeter and the main driver to indicate when they're on. These LEDs are bright. I put black duck tape over them for a few days when I was watching movies from bed and the only lights in the room were the computer monitor and these speaker power lights. It just bugged me mildly. It's not the kind of bright that's painful to look at, but these blue LEDs could distract from the overall aesthetic of your build or your desk set up, especially if blue clashes with your color scheme.

Don't expect them to get close to a proper set of 5" or 6" bookshelf speakers, but in my opinion the sound easily beats anything that Logitech or Creative sell at this size. They can easily blast music in a small/medium room, and they're great for gaming at your desk.
Build quality is also fantastic. The speakers come out of the box looking perfect. They have a very dense feel to them, and the paint finish is perfect all the way around. The volume knob (while inconveniently on the back) feels fantastic.
My main gripe with the speakers is the lack of a dedicated remote or controls to switch between inputs (it's just done automatically). This means you can't specifically turn Bluetooth off, or disable the USB input. For my use case (just using RCA) it isn't a problem though.
If you can grab these on sale I think it's worth it, but you might be able to match the sound quality with something like a Steelseries Arena. If you want something that looks fantastic on your desk, go no further.

name: Gigabyte GAMING OC Radeon RX 9070 XT 16 GB Video Card
comments:
This was the purchase that triggered the build. I think I bagged the last 9070xt in the UK on launch day!
Great GPU, and out of the box it's very quiet. 3D Mark scores are above average for the 9070xt. I ended up underclocking it a bit to save on power. I managed to get a -40mV undervolt combined with a -500MHz underclock and -10% power limit and it runs very cool and quiet, and I'm still getting average 3D mark scores!
Other 9070xt models can get a better undervolt, I maybe didn't win the silicon lottery, but its still an impressive display for a lower-end 9070xt model.
Note that this model requires THREE PCIe 8-pin connectors. My PSU had exactly three, but two of the connectors are daisy chained. THIS IS OKAY! I've had zero issues with the daisy chained PCIe connector since installation, and it's been through a lot of stress tests.
BEWARE GIGABYTE CONTROL CENTER!
Because I have a Gigabyte motherboard and a Gigabyte GPU, I downloaded Gigabyte Control Center to control the RGB. This works fine, but one of the other tools (I think maybe the performance tool plugin?) took control of the fan curve, which was ATTROCIOUS. The card's sweet spot for temperature is around 75°C, and at that temperature Gigabyte's default fan curve puts the fans at 100%, which is abour 4000RPM. It's LOUD. Once I uninstalled the fan control tools, the default fan curve is infinitely quieter.
The other fan curves for CPU and case fans/pumps are all editable in the BIOS. A bit inconvenient, but the Gigabyte Control Center app doesn't provide any additional functionality.

Got this at launch for Gigabyte's standard price of 730. I'd rather pay MSRP, but we all know that's a thing of the past. At least I didn't have to pay scalper prices.
My other PC has a 7900xtx in it and I would say that this GPU keeps up with it well. With ray tracing enabled it seems to do a little better in the games that I play. I personally don't care for ray tracing, but I know that many do. In my ITX case the card runs at 60 under a load with the hot spot just breaking 80.
All in all I'm very happy with the performance for the price I paid.

I upgraded from a GTX 1660Ti laptop version to this RTX 4060 desktop, and the performance difference is INSANE. I can play Helldivers 2 at 1080p Medium-High Graphic Settings at 120 FPS no issue, Fortnite on DX12 with High settings at 144FPS (without ray-tracing) and 280-300fps on the performance mode. Rocket league is a stable 240 fps at max settings (with a maximum of 300fps from my experience), Minecraft: Java Edition at max240 fps with an avg of 140-180fps with 16 render chunks, with Sodium and all those fabric mods installed, and at around 90-120 fps with shaders at that same render distance.
All those FPS listings above was while the card was remaining under an 80C temp. I average about 73-78C on most games. Highest I've gone is 83C on CS2 at around 300 FPS on High settings. I highly recommend this card to any budget builder that can afford this in their budget if possible. I would personally recommend this over the 3060 (8 or 12GB version) because of the lower power consumption while remaining the same performance.
If you want a 12 GB card that badly, I recommend looking at GPUs rated for 1440p rather than 1080p. Such as:
RX 6750XT
RX 6700XT
RX 7700XT
RTX 4070
RTX 4070 Super

Well, it’s been a wild couple of months for the GPU market, again. The new generation of cards is being massively gouged, and the old generation is shooting up in price. So, how does my latest acquisition hold up? Pretty well, to put it plainly. My B580 was on backorder since the end of 2024, and I had it in hand a month later for Intel’s suggested retail price. I’ve always liked slightly odd peripherals, and Intel’s previous forays into the GPU market have certainly been awkward.
On the hardware side, it ticks all the boxes for decent longevity. The industrial design of the shell is perennial—a black plastic rectangle bereft of aggressive angular lines, rainbow LEDs, or the military foot-locker aesthetic board partners seem to love. The specs are great for the price—trading blows with the 4060 Ti and 7600 XT. Best of all, the thermals and potential for overclocking have been solid.
Intel’s software is Radeon-tier, in my opinion. A little better organized than AMD’s offerings, but with fewer features. Some options aren’t explained clearly, and the ability to reduce the card’s voltage below stock settings just doesn’t exist. A lot of third-party tuning software (such as Afterburner) also struggles with Intel’s architecture.
“Radeon-like” sums up much of the Battlemage experience, as there’s significant overlap between the brands. Vulkan support isn’t just optional for this card—it’s preferable. Linux support shouldn’t be a matter of if but when. And unless XeSS catches on in more games, FSR 3.1 is the best way to upscale most titles.
With Intel’s limited track record in the dedicated graphics business, it’s hard to say exactly how well this card will age. But I think it’s a great deal for the tumultuous present.

name: Sapphire PULSE Radeon RX 7600 XT 16 GB Video Card
comments: I've got to say I am very impressed with this card. It gets a lot of flak from rich youtubers and reviewers online, but its a solid card. I play primarily AAA titles, old and new. I'm not much of an E sport gamer so I don't care all that much about fps. This card is able to play games like RDR2, the Tomb Raider reboots, and TLOU1 at 1440P max settings with 60FPS. For the very demanding games like TLOU1 you do need frame gen to keep that 60FPS stable but for everything else I mentioned and games similar to it, it chews through them at native 1440 just fine. I did notice some FPS fluctuation in Tomb Raider 2013, but its most likely due to that games PC port not being all that optimized being over a decade old. The big kicker on this card is the large 16GB memory buffer, it severely helps at 1440P and is the reason why its even able to game at that higher resolution. Despite what folks say, its not useless. Its got about a 288GB memory bandwidth which is on the higher side for the 128 bit bus and is more than adequate for 1440P gaming. Again, I see no issues and got the card for a bit more than an RTX 4060 and I'm loving it. Temps are good, the fans nice and quiet, the card has good thermals, and it's just about 2 slots so it fits perfectly into my SFF console sized case. At MSRP for 30 bucks more than an NVIDIA 4060 the card is incredible value and its awesome that you can get into high fidelity 1440P gaming for sub 350 bucks
Excellent for 1080p but struggles a bit on 1440p. Otherwise pretty cheap for a 16gb gpu.

[Fan Tuning]:

Advanced Control: Enabled
[GPU Tuning]:
Advanced Control: Enabled
Min Frequency: 500
Max Frequency: 3100
Voltage: 990
[Power Tuning]:
Power Limit: 15%
[VRAM Tuning]:

Advanced Control: Enabled
Max Frequency: 2568

comments: great card, runs 1440p on high settings and 20 VRAM is great future proofing

Got this card for $700 at Microcenter, and at that price the 7900XT is a pretty decent buy for the performance. However, there definitely are a few issues I have with card, starting with a reference model specific issue regarding memory junction temperatures; If the GPU core temperature is 60C, the memory junction temp is usually at 84C, which is a 24C delta between the two. This drastic difference in temperature seems to be a flaw with the reference designs only, and so should be solved with AIB models.
Although the total board power was 315W max as expected, I found that the card also tried to boost all the way to 2900MHz, which is 500MHz past the advertised boost clock! Under this behavior the "GPU power maximum" reading in HWinfo64 could reach all the way to 500W, which was just unsettling. What compounds this issue is the fact that the card has very bad coil whine when it tries to boost to such high clocks. And so to optimize the card I simply limited the clock to 2400MHz, increased the memory clock to 2714MHz, increased the power limit to +15%, and undervolted it to 1030mV. With these settings, I only lost 5% of the stock performance while consuming a lot less power on average (315W down to sub-250W) and greatly silenced the coil whine. If the card shipped like this at stock I would have probably given it 5 stars with the only caveat being the high but not dangerous memory junction temperatures.

comments:
This card is one of the few 9070 XTs advertised as reaching 3100 rather than 3060 MHz boost clocks, alongside the ASRock Taichi and some XFX cards. Interestingly, the Aorus and Taichi are also the cheapest 9070 XT flagship cards. With out of the box settings it actually boosted to 3150 MHz. This card has a vapour chamber, dual bios, and uses 3x8pin, so on paper the only downside is that it doesn't use PTM7950.
Cooling is excellent as would be expected from the massive heatsink, and the default fan curve prioritizes lower fan speed over lower temps, with fans not even beginning to spin until the hotspot reaches 50 degrees, and usually spinning at around 1000 rpm (max ~3500) unless temps heavily increase. With a relatively quiet fan curve hot spot temp remains below 65 degrees and VRAM below 75. Running fans at max speed without sharply increasing case fan speeds during benchmarks with overclocked VRAM, speeds over 3300 MHz and +10% power limit the highest temperatures I noticed were 78 degrees on the hot spot and 86 degrees on the VRAM. More than adequate performance given the task and well below thermal limits.
Speculative, but I also suspect that these cards are very aggressively binned, moreso than any other 9070 XT model. At first I noticed that my card was an absolute silicon lottery win, reaching #3 Port Royal, #5 Steel Nomad DX12, and #9 Time Spy Graphics Score on the 3DMark 9070 XT leaderboards. A friend with another Aorus 9070 XT also got relatively high scores, and I saw another example online. I checked the 3DMark leaderboards again and noticed that 5 of the top 10 Time Spy graphics scores were Gigabyte cards, 5 of the top 10 Port Royal scores were Gigabyte cards, and 6 out of the top 10 Steel Nomad scores were Gigabyte cards. With Gigabyte being a second tier AMD AIB, the overrepresentation in benchmark scores, the Aorus being one of the few 3100 MHz cards, and that Gigabyte Gaming OCs seem much more common than Gigabyte Aorus cards, I think it's very possible that Gigabyte is aggressively binning both the GPU chips and VRAM that goes into their Aorus cards.
Got this for $1020 CAD ($710 USD) when "MSRP" models were selling for around $950 CAD. Unless it was confirmed Aorus 9070 XTs are all aggressively binned I would not rate 5 stars if pricing improved on other 9070 XT models, 5070 Tis, or price went up on this card.

comments: For cooling, I went with the Liquid Freezer III 360. This is my first AIO, and so far, I'm very pleased with it. I replaced the stock fans with three Arctic P12 MAX, which probably hasn't made any real difference. Maybe it's a little louder than stock; I don't know. I had heard that the mounting onto the mobo would be a little tricky, but I experienced no problems at all with the installation .
Keeps 7800X3D cool under load, good value

Bought for 90 USD from Amazon in January 2025. Planned on getting a Phantom Spirit 120 Evo, but reconsidered seeing various great reviews for this AIO for $40 more. Runs very quiet and is overkill for my current CPU (so I've been told), though still am considering an air cooler in the future.
Keeps temps right where they should be!
Keeps my CPU cool, but the mounting process is a bit unclear

Best value cooler for power hungry chips imo. No rgb, no ******** displays, just a beefy thick radiator. Keeps a 253 watt 14900k under 70°. The installation on Intel is a breeze, no extreme pressure or force required. The pump is somewhat noisy at 100% speed, but it is PWM controlled and can be slowed down significantly with a fan curve. Stock fans connection that goes through the tubes is weird as it only has 2 pins. I ended up wiring the fans myself with a proper 4 pin cable. VRM fan is comically small, but I guess it does... something. At least it is quiet even at full rpm.
Really effective, but its a big beefy cooler. Literally bigger than my GPU

Clearly very capable. I had a little trouble mounting the block onto the CPU mounts. I suspect the mounting brackets have a tiny bit of play when screwing in, so they weren't weren't exactly perfectly positioned on my first attempt. This stopped the block from screwing in. Would've liked more than 0.8g of MX-6, but this is adequate for at least a couple applications. Super pricing.
I checked compatibility with the motherboard before purchasing. Highly recommended to do so beforehand as the pump/waterblock can be impeded by high VRM and/or NVME SSD heatsinks.

The best AIO out there, while also one of the cheapest? Count me in. Keeps my overclocked + undervolted 9800X3D below 60c while gaming. Only drawback, but I won’t take off a start for that, is its mounting mechanism. Could be easier. My suggestion is, mount the 2x provided black metal rails ON THE PUMP first, and then try mounting all the thing on the motherboard, not the opposite way (which is what the manual says). If you go with what the manual says, the screws on the pump will NEVER reach the metal rails.
Good n' cheap.

Nice and quiet, I don’t think I can hear it up until about 50 percent fan speed which is barely ever. Seemed to be really good value too.

Easy to install, keeps my CPU cool under stress, and looks great in my case. What more could you ask for? I think it brings a tasteful level of RGB without going overboard. And for how cheap it is, it's a great value.
Its cheap, looks cool, lights up, and keeps my cpu plenty cool.

Got the RGB one because it was cheaper at the time. Replaced the middle fan with a P12 Max and at the side (over the RAM) only a slim one could fit without touching the cables that power the MOBO. Needed to dremmel the side bracket that holds the Noctua fan a little bit so the heatpipes didn't touch it, but it fits perfectly apart from that.

I chose this over ID Cooling's A620 Pro SE even though the PS120SE costs $5 more just because I did not like the build quality of the former unit.
AFAIK, Frost Spirit > Frost Commander > Phantom Spirit > Peerless Assassin. "SE" models have a small height difference (e.g. 154 mm vs 157 mm in heatsink specs for PS120SE vs PS120) but perform the same (fan specs/noise level/air flow et al.) and are cheaper. Just pick from any of the 4 models that fits in your budget and/or build aesthetic.
Refer:
What's the difference between all these Thermalright coolers?
It is a non-issue for me but I did notice that I had to put more pressure installing this cooler as compared to other CPU coolers I have installed in the past. Still, documenting here for posterity.
I had no issues with RAM clearance. Just check the dimensions of whatever RAM + CPU cooler combination you select. Thermalright's website might be lacking in design but they are very upfront about their product specs and do not hide anything from you.

I came across the cooler on my own as I knew I wanted a fan and not water cooled. After I did some research I found out that this is a really popular cooler. The price is amazing! Performance reviews showed that it was a really good cooler for half the price as its competitors. Easy to install. It does come with its own thermal paste but I used Arctic MX-6 paste instead. The size is a bit on the large end so I had to get low profile RAM stick for it to fit under the cooler's fan. Keeps my CPU temps very cool even under a load. I am now an advocate for the Thermalright brand.

This is one of highest value CPU coolers you can buy for $48CAD. It keeps my 7600x very cool~50°C under load and the fans are quiet. The only minor downside is the length of the ARGB cable. It is NOT long enough to run up and over the motherboard, behind and up from the bottom with a mATX motherboard. However, thanks to the coolers size, I could run it down the front of the motherboard and behind the graphics card without it being visible. Also, no matter what I do in the BIOS to the fan curves, it is impossible to make them stop spinning when idle. That might just be a skill issue though. This cooler fits in the NZXT H5 Flow 2023 with the front fan raised by ~5mm due to RAM clearance with a G Skill Trident RGB kit.
Great at cooling, but it takes up quite a bit of space. Regardless it's easy to set up and gets the job done!

Overall, a great wind cooler that still performs as good or even better than many water coolers out there for a great price.

It's quiet and does a great job of controlling heat.

The lack of cables and ease of installation is a massive pro. It's whisper silent, with not a ton of weird pump noise that I seem to hear a lot in lianli and NZXT AIOs. Super quiet and for the price, punches well above its weight class.

I really thought I'd need a better cooler for my 9900X, but it turns out the Arctic Freezer III is built different. My 9900X idles at ~40C and never goes above 75C during load. According to reviewers this the best aio performance you can get on AM5.

I'm not sure about this cooler yet. For the price, absolutely a home-run. Install instructions are lacking at best. Let me explain:
I am questioning the AM5 mounting system for this cooler. The instructions say to install the water block bracket at an angle, line up the arrow on the block and the bracket and rotate clock-wise to secure it. Well, when I rotate the bracket, it doesn't lock in, rather it just sits in the block and will slide out and fall off the block very easily if you don't physically hold it on. This became an issue when it came time to install the block onto my CPU. As I stated already, it likes to rotate out and fall off since it won't lock in place. I was still able to install it, but I had to hold the bracket in place to prevent it from moving while I mounted the block to the CPU. Interestingly this cooler uses the factory mounting brackets that come on AMD motherboards, don't often see that, but it made installing the water block super easy minus the bracket issue.
So, since the bracket won't lock in properly, it makes the LED logo on the block look crooked, or un-level. This can't be the correct way to install the water block if you ask me. So far temps don't seem too bad, but I need to get a second monitor to check the real-time temps while I play a few games. So far it idles around 45-47C.
LEDs on the fans look good, fans are quiet enough. They're not Noctua or Be Quiet! fans, but they are certainly serviceable. Corsair iCUE LINK TITAN 360 Review: Cooling Power With Style If you’re looking for a cooler that can keep up with your high-end gaming or streaming setup, the Corsair iCUE LINK TITAN 360 is here to blow you away. This thing packs a huge 360mm radiator, three beastly 120mm fans, and all the cool features you need to take your PC’s cooling to the next level—while looking awesome while doing it.
Seriously Powerful Cooling Let’s talk performance: the 360mm radiator means this cooler is built for heavy-duty cooling. Whether you’re pushing your CPU to the max with overclocking or gaming for hours, the three 120mm fans have got your back, keeping your rig cool and stable even under the most intense workloads.
Easy Control with iCUE One of the best things about this cooler is its iCUE integration. If you’re already familiar with Corsair’s iCUE software, you know it’s a game-changer. With iCUE, you can easily control fan speeds, RGB lighting, and even pump speeds all from your PC. Want to switch up the look of your system? Just use iCUE to play with the RGB effects—whether you want a chill vibe or a full-blown light show, it’s all at your fingertips.
Simple Installation Despite its massive 360mm radiator, the iCUE LINK TITAN 360 is actually pretty easy to install. Corsair’s tool-free mounting system makes it simple to get the cooler set up quickly, and the flexible tubing means you won’t be struggling to fit it into your case. Plus, the anti-vibration mounts keep everything nice and steady, making sure the cooler stays quiet.
Quiet But Mighty What’s impressive about this cooler is that, even though it’s packing some serious cooling power, it’s still super quiet. The fans run quietly when your system is chilling, but when you’re pushing your rig, they ramp up and keep the noise levels in check. It's like having all the performance without the noise.
Final Thoughts: A Killer Cooler With a Clean Look The Corsair iCUE LINK TITAN 360 is everything you need in a cooler: serious performance, easy control, and killer looks. If you’re building a high-performance rig and want something that can handle the heat while also looking awesome, this cooler is a no-brainer.

Pros:
38mm thick radiator provides more cooling then standard thickness radiators
VRM fan is actually effective
The leaf spring on the pump provides nice pressure on the CPU
Comes with a contact frame for Intel Chips
Comes with offset bracket mount for AM5 chips
The tubes are nice and long, allowing this to be mounted to the top or side of a case
Cons:
The pump can be a pain to get mounted into the AM5 offset bracket mount due to the leaf spring
On the underside of the brackets for AM5 chips are tiny paper thin nuts stamped/formed into the metal of the bracket. If you tighten down the pump to much or to hard it will break those nuts and allow them to spin freely, making it impossible to get the pump off without undoing the entire bracket system. (I had to buy another one of these because of that issue)
Minor Grievances:
The pump and hoses coming from it may have clearance issues with certain motherboards (Ex. ASUS X870E HERO and it's top most M.2 Heatsink)
The cables for the fans and the RGB run up one of the hoses and connect to the included RGB fans. If you are using different fans these cables may be redundant and are very hard to hide.
The tubes used are hard and don't like to bend a lot
The included cables for the RGB on the VRM header and to power the pump and fans are long making cable management a bit difficult
Final Thoughts:
I would recommend this to anyone who wants a 420mm AIO liquid cooler for their system. Arctic makes some very nice liquid coolers with excellent cooling to price performance. The leaf spring design for the Liquid Freezer III series is nice but also a pain, especially if you are on an AM5 chip. The inclusion of a contact frame for Intel chips is a nice touch from Arctic. The offset brackets for AM5 chips could use a revision. As mentioned above, there are tiny paper thin nuts on the underside of the bracket where the pump screws into. If you screw down the pump to tight or to hard (which is easy to do because of the leaf spring used), those tiny nuts will break and spin freely. Which makes it impossible to get the pump off and you will have to undo the entire bracket system to get the pump off. I had this happen to the first one I bought and I had to buy a new one.
Great cooler, working well so far.

Does not handle quick cpu temp fluctuations from sudden loads very well, will jump from 40c to low 50c quickly. But under extended heavy loads it has never allowed the 7600X3D to get over 77c. 4 stars because this thing is a bear and a half to mount properly while solo. The screws on the mounting hardware are a pain to get started, you need enough force to bend the spring steel tension plate to get the screws started, but not so much that you cause thermal paste to thin out on the cpu... A different mount solution or an installation aid would be much appreciated in future releases.

Generally they are one of the best, if not the best performing AIOs on the market with the others being Lian Li GA II Trinity and EKWB EK-Nucleus. Unfortunately EK seems to be on the economic ropes right now and may not survive. Some YouTube tech channels have cut ties with them due to their business practices. Lian Li has always been good, their RMA and customer support has been great, although I have had two of their AIOs fail on me. So, that leaves Arctic as the most, at this point, reliable. This model is an improved model for them. I think it is a better aesthetic design and easy to install. It's also inexpensive relative to other AIOs.
For me, also, they are one of the few companies offering a 420mm radiator. So, that was really the deciding factor.

Price was a little high, the 4 double sided screws can be a little tricky, it provides exceptional performances, runs quiet, AIO and RGB look amazing.
The Kraken elite was a good pick for the CPU that I bought. It was a little pricey compared to most other cpu coolers, but I couldn't get my hands on the Arctic II unfortunately, so I settled for good performance for a hefty price. First off, it looks great, it doesn't run super loud, and when I need it to kick on and cool off my Ryzen 9 7950x when it reaches those high temps, it does so. The cable management for it was pretty easy, at least with this version, there's not so many cables that are kind of in the way, it looks very neat and the whole thing was easy to put together with the single case fan. There was a 3 prong cable that came off of the CPU cooler that I didn't end up hooking into anything, and it still runs fine.
It had an Intel and AMD version for the AIO to connect to your motherboard. It came already installed with the Intel bracket, I had to switch it out for the AMD bracket and make sure to be careful not to bump into the Pre-applied thermal paste. It's nice that they include both versions and they are very easy to switch out. I will say 4 screws are double sided for connecting to the motherboard and at first glance they have the same thread but they do not, make sure you install it correctly. The pre-applied thermal paste on the bottom of the AIO was also super nice, you just have to be careful not to bump into it at all when you set it down in your CPU and let it go. And the AIO itself is beautiful, the customization is awesome, people give NZXT a real hard time with their software but I think if you understand computer software, it's not that hard.
A little pricey but went with NZXT on a lot of the computer components so felt necessary to get the Kraken Elite. Worth the price though this cooler is beautiful and powerful.

Pros: Big and beautiful display with a lot of customization options. The cordless design on the pump looks very clean. The Kraken Elite V2 also has great performance keeping my 13900K ~8c cooler than my previous Corsair H150i Elite AIO under stress testing.
Cons: The pump has a rattle/grinding sound when set to less than 40% speed (~1900rpm or less). I never have my pump set that low so it's not much of an issue, but I have read it's pretty common, so something to keep in mind.
The 2.7 inch LCD screen is awesome with gif feature. It has some coil whine under load, but acceptable.

comments: This is an amazing CPU! It also provided a 20% uplift in Cinebench R24 (both CPUs running with the Auto Overclock), which I didn't expect given the core count difference. The only issue I've found is that it runs really hot. I'm not sure if I need to reinstall my AIO or what, but in the same case with the same 360mm AIO, the 9800X3D can reach over 90 degrees under a heavy load, whereas my 5900x never exceeded 60 degrees. That's a huge difference, certainly more than I expected.

Cinebench 2024 scores without any undervolt/overclock applied:
Multi Core: 1292 pts
Single Core: 130 pts
I was able to purchase this CPU in a bundle with the MSI MEG X670E ACE motherboard directly off of MSI's website. Not only did the bundle lower the cost of the 9800X3D ($435 as opposed to Amazon's $479), but I was also able to stack a 5% coupon code on top of the total cost of the bundle at the time. At the risk of sounding like an ad for MSI at this point, there was also no sales tax while shopping on their website :D
Side note - in the picture I posted of all of the individual parts, the AMD box is missing because it's not included when you purchase the CPU as part of a bundle. Instead, it comes in the small plastic casing and taped to the exterior of the motherboard box.

12/2/2024 Update: I just completed my bios update and was able to get a new processor from intel for free due to the instability flaw. I had no issues the first 6 months then it started to crash in certain games. (Helldivers, Forza, and BF2042), then I started to get random BSOD. I would bench test it and it would always pass 100%, I then would use the Intel Extreme tuner to dial down the Performance Ratio down by 3 and it never crashed after that. I finally contacted Intel customer support and opened a ticket and after several rounds of questions they agree to send me a new CPU. You have to pay $25 out of pocket for processing and then you must pay $600 for the replacement CPU, which they will fully refund once they receive the old/damaged one back. No BSOD and running at full ratio, so I guess I did have flawed CPU. And yes it runs hot, but seems to have gone down after reapplying thermal paste with the Noctua brand. On the bright side of things, I have been playing Stalker 2 on epic settings and have zero problems and everyone seems to have a ton of problems playing it.
Pro Tip: when cleaning up the old thermal paste, use the silver intel disk for packaging as tray to clean your pump head on so no debris falls into your case.
Knowing an Intel employee we managed to get it for cheaper, and basically guaranteed help/replacement if anything goes wrong. So far so good, runs fast no issues.

I don't usually review components in my builds, but for this processor I'll make an exception. This processor had initially been used for another computer, but something had gone wrong and the computer was showing signs of severe instability with blue screens and bootloops during startup. In the bios settings I had set the Intel settings by default, while later I had set automatic overclocking and activated XMP for the RAM memories. Thinking that the processor was faulty, I replaced it with another one, effectively obtaining a more stable system. At this point I thought that my Core i9 14900k was to be thrown away, given that the useful period for a possible return had already passed, but I wanted to give it a second chance by reusing it for this build. This time I wanted to keep the Intel settings, without imposing any changes in the bios, to understand if the processor was actually defective or not. Well, to my great surprise and relief, I was able to notice that not only was the 14900k fully functional, but that, without losing efficiency and speed, it had very low operating temperatures, which allowed me to have an extremely silent system. Now, it's clear that all this depends on Intel's highly limiting settings, but for me, since I don't use the PC to play, it's not that serious. All I need is for the computer to work well and smoothly. It's a real shame, however, to see Intel make these design errors and thus diminish the prestige it has worked hard to earn over the years... Having said that, I just wanted to testify to my experience with what I believe to be one of the most powerful processors currently on the market. Let's hope that Intel has learned its lesson and doesn't repeat the same mistakes with the next CPUs.

I could have gone with a newer Gen CPU, but I kind of saw this one, and I think for my budget and saving 300$, this one brings a very high level of performance and can keep up with the newer gen systems at an affordable price. I will add that your general room temperature plays a huge role in how hot this thing can get, if your room is warmer because its summer time then it might get very hot duh.
Overkill in the best way
A BEHEMOTH of a processor. Eats what I needs it to do and processes it before eating. Doesn't make sense, I know but it is just fast. REALLY fast. REALLY REALLY fast.
This thing is an absolute monster, runs cool and so far is doing amazingly, definitely worth it over the more expensive 9950x which has worse gaming performance also
Perfect for everything at a pretty good price too. Will handle pretty much anything

After reading all the reviews and watching videos about this generation of CPUs getting very hot, I decided that I still wanted to upgrade to this generation and I'm glad I did. This CPU does get hot but the NZXT Kraken Elite AIO cools it very well.
Lightning fast CPU, never broke a sweat playing at 4k on Cyberpunk or while editing videos on AE.

name: Intel Core i3-12100F 3.3 GHz Quad-Core Processor
comments: Im surprised intel still makes quad core chips to this day. Not complaining though. Can upgrade even though socket is dead. This thing packs a punch even though it's quad core.
Best price to performance intel CPU. If I wanted higher performance and had a higher budget I would of went AMD. out of all the price ranges, this is the only Intel CPU that beats AMD.

For the price it was a no brainer at the time, the i5 and Ryzen 5600 (3600 or Ryzen 3 were not options) were too expensive, and the performance really does not dissapoint. I'd consider upgrading if possible, but it's not necessary.
Excellent value processor which is still more than capable in 1080 gaming and everyday tasks. The main advantage is its price and low TDP of only 65W.
Solid little gaming beast for under $100

The 12100f features the Alder Lake micro-architecture and has quad core design. It is an entry level processor, but performs well in benchmarks and can give older quad core i5s and i7s a tough challenge, or even outright beat them. It achieved a great score in Cinebench R23, with multi-core performance at 8138 points, and single core performance at 1586 points.
With that being said, it is still an entry level processor, only having 4c/8t comparing to other budget options such as the Ryzen 5 5500 (Having 6c/12t), Ryzen 5 5600G(6c/12t) and the i5-12400f (6c/12t). Still have stellar gaming performance, but there are other options avaliable. Price to performance is amazing.

For the price, the i3 12100F is incredible value. I bought it at $95 but it can drop to $85, which is even better. Strongly recommend for those that want to put together a system on a tight budget, especially over the 13100F and 14100F, since the performance uplift isn't notable, yet they cost much more.
Keep in mind that I bought this CPU in March/April before the news with Intel's 13th and 14th gen chips being unstable on higher end SKUs. I can't say I recommend buying into LGA 1700 anymore, but please do your research.
Also, make sure to get a CPU contact frame to prevent motherboard warping! I have a Thermalright contact frame and it works great (good price point too).
It will bottleneck in games like Cyberpunk but for easy to run games it's perfect. Using it with RX 6600. Hard to beat for the price. Only needs around 50W so it stays cool.

Decent price & performance. Comes with finally a somewhat acceptable stock cooler (Intel Laminar Coolers), has nice single core performance. It is a really bad CPU for anything multicore, as it's only a 4/8 CPU.
amazing cpu for it price it does kinda bottleneck my 1080ti but its fine

name: AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D 4.4 GHz 12-Core Processor
AMD Ryzen 7 5700G 3.8 GHz 8-Core Processor
comments: Fine cpu

Great it took the place while waiting for the GPU...
It does its job nicely...
Good cpu I recommend a better CPU for games like BeamNG.drive
Great CPU for general gaming For games like BeamNG.drive I would recommend something stronger
Great 8-core Radeon graphics cpu with a nice clock. And only 180 USD!!
Great cpu with surprisingly good integrated graphics. Not much else to say about it

I got this CPU cause I wanted something decent with 8 cores and an iGPU, specifically so if my GPU were to die for whatever reason, I could still have something to help my play games, if even a little bit. Worth the 170$ I paid but don't think it'd quite be worth the ~330$ I've seen it going for
Honestly this part doesn't make a whole lot of sense for anything other than what I'm using it for. But for what I'm using it for current pricing is a great value.

I chose the AMD Ryzen 7 5700G for my CPU, for its iGPU is more than enough for Minecraft and Roblox. A dedicated GPU would have significantly reduced the CPU I could get with my ~$500 budget. With 8 cores and 16 threads, I can easily have many applications open at once, including a MySQL database and Apache webserver. I've also been able to run a Minecraft server and multiple Discord bot without a problem.
Decent I gpu and oc power.

name: Intel Core i9-12900K 3.2 GHz 16-Core Processor
comments: No problems apart the fact that it gets really hot and it's usual for intel cpus for some reason.

A little older CPU as my main rig runs an i7 12700k. But when it comes to performance for production workloads this thing is still up there with Ryzen 7 and Intel Core Ultra CPUs, and since this is mostly used for music, 3D modeling, and video editing this was a huge point to me. Just make sure your cooling solution is efficient, real easy to hit the 'tj max' on this CPU and thermal throttle at 99°C.
Absolute beast of a CPU, good for gaming and multi-tasking, and can be found for a pretty decent price at times.
Runs fast and stays decently cool. No issues like the 13 and 14 gen cpu's have.
This CPU served me well, in my main rig I upgraded to the 14900k, so this was just not being used.
Got this as part of a bundle of FB marketplace. Its definitely a mighty chip but it runs hot and a 280mm AIO is just barely covering it. If you can keep it cool it does its job well!
Runs at 76C while under full load for 10 minutes with a 360mm AIO. It's also super fast and works great with my 4070 Super.
Fast and runs pretty cool under a 360mm aio
Killer CPU. Especially if you can get it used. Worth the price for the highest end 12th gen you can get. Don't have to worry about 13th & 14th gen issues either :)
Best you can get right now without stability issues. 10/10.

name: AMD Ryzen 5 8600G 4.3 GHz 6-Core Processor
comments: The 8600G is one of the fastest APUs in the current market. The iGPU offers graphics performance comparable to the Nvidia GeForce GTX 1630 and AMD Radeon HD 7950 (per TechPowerUp). The iCPU offers processing performance comparable to the Intel i5 12400 and the AMD Ryzen 5 5600X. Not a bad CPU/GPU combo for a little over US$150 total.
It's a great processor for a good price and the integrated graphics is just a bonus in case you might need it, or if for whatever reason what you do doesn't require a graphics card.
A good APU for light 1080p gaming, although a bit weak at times.

It's definitely the best APU on the market. Its gaming performance is wonderful, even with integrated graphics. Along with 32gb of RAM at 6000 MT/s (8gb VRAM), I have been able to play games like RDR2 at 50 FPS with medium/high graphics settings. This processor is the perfect choice for a BUDGET PC (<550 USD) aimed at gaming.
Works great
i wanted the 8700g but i couldn't afford it... this cpu is rly not far off though, the 760m runs games shockingly well😊
-- really good igpu, runs most games well even without a dedicated gpu!
Excellent speed, low power consumption and low heat. Using separate graphics card in my build and not the integrated gpu.
Great cpu to buy when on sale, and even works perfectly fine with a dedicated mid tier GPU

If you game lightly and play light games (ie: Fortnite), and only want 1080p 60fps, then this cpu is perfect for you. I also got it on a CAD$40 discount so that made it even better. If you want to play AAA games however, you will probably need to buy a gpu.

name: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D 4.2 GHz 16-Core Processor
comments: Killer CPU, perfect for my situation where I'm gaming, have virtual machines running, and have DAWs with multiple plugins running, often all of these at the same time since I don't like having to close everything when I'm going to game. It's a hot one, so make sure to get proper cooling for it.

Pricey, but it hits everything I was looking for in this build, I have not seen any data so far to show the 9950X3D will significantly outperform this. In my opinion, it will likely run cooler, use less power and have the ability to match if not outperform any needs I have over the next 2-3 years..

An absolute beast of a CPU, probably overkill for my use cases but I managed to grab an amazingly cheap bundle at Microcenter back when 7800x3d stock was nonexistent and before the 9800x3d dropped. While I mostly game with it, the occasional computational workload is handled with ease.
Absolute beast, I really appreciate having more cores compared to the Ryzen 7s and similar performance!
This CPU is a BEAST for any task such as gaming or rendering or just every day use!
Basically got it for $350 thanks to my 7800x3D RMA. Its just a 7800x3D with 8 extra cores so you can do anything you think of on it. Enables me to get my 360hz @ 1440p with ease.
Half V-cache, half without. But I suppose you already knew that. It works.
Amazing for gaming and multitasking folks!
It takes everything I throw at it what else is there to say.
Does the job perfectly for gaming and multi-task projects in late 2024 (3D modelling, coding, etc.)

name: AMD Ryzen 7 5800XT 3.8 GHz 8-Core Processor
comments: None of that 3D cache magic that the 5700X3D and 5800X3D have going on. But my 5800XT was only $140. In terms of non-gaming raw performance, it technically outperforms the 5800X3D too. After all, it's got the highest single threaded performance out of any AM4 CPU, according to Passmark at least. But it's also a very toasty chip. Reminds me of AMD's 220W FX-9590 days.

name: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 3.4 GHz 16-Core Processor
comments: Beastly cpu, but runs HOT. Run it downclocked to 4.5Ghz max and undervolted with a -20 Curve Optimizer offset. Since I game at 60-75fps at 1440p, single core speed at 4.5 is fine. Main thing I wanted was multi-threaded performance in Handbrake, Da Vinci Resolve and Topaz AI apps, and it absolutely delivers.

"Get'er DONE!!!!"
Works Great
Really good
Great CPU with a lotta threads, I love AM4!

CPU core undervolted with offset mode of 0.15 and platform thermal throttle limit set to 70C. PBO disabled. In an ambient room temperature of about 26C, I am getting a base clock speed of around 3.6 GHz and a maximum boost of about 4.7 GHz.
It only runs hot if your doing major high end gaming or workloads but i have not seen it go past 83c at full load. Just make sure you have adequate cooling.
It's not a huge upgrade, but the extra cores and thread come in handy for virtual machines. Gentoo Linux compiles will go faster because there will be more resources available.
Great CPU. Uses some power. Proper settings can get good performance and contain the heat.

name: Intel Core i9-14900KF 3.2 GHz 24-Core Processor
comments: Despite the Intel hate and its issues, I had gone with it anyway. It works fine for gaming, and productivity, yet I wonder how long it will last since the BIOS "fix" didn't really fix it for most people. And unfortunately I bought a dead socket, so no future upgrading :(

For due diligence, I did a deep dive into Intel’s over-volting & oxidation problem. Although I haven’t experienced any issues. I do consider myself lucky. There’s a lot of contradictory information about this online though. & while It was hard to parse out what was opinion or fact. I’m certainly not the only one who’s had a positive experience with the 14th series. But, I digress; your experience may vary. Ultimately, I decided I’d stick to Intel defaults & implement an offset.

Very fast CPU. I have had no problems with it. Just remember to update your BIOS to the new fix Intel put out to keep your CPU from exploding. Only downside is you cannot overclock this CPU because the fix for it, was to essentially underpower it. However it is very powerful and no game has even remotely come close to maxing this CPU out.
Good cpu, does everything I need, the instability problems did not affect me at all, but I got the BIOS update that fixes the instability to make sure.
Hasn't crashed yet, and performs great
Got it with MSI bundle deal along with the Ace motherboard. It was an OEM part so no box or packaging. So far so good with temp. I used Intel AI tool for overclock, again no issues.
Runs well, puts out power, no problems with it.

Just get the K, no F, even if you are getting a standalone video card. The integrated graphics and the separate GPU actually work together. Other than that, blazing fast, but also blazing hot. For general use in a creator PC, you might not be thermally limited with an air cooler, but for heavy 3D or gaming you'll need a big AIO. Also jeeeez they're not kidding about the flaws with LGA 1700's mounting systems! I stalled in a hot sweat for like 20 minutes on this build, because I just could not believe the amount of pressure I was having to apply to get that wonky lever down, with the bracket holding the CPU in the socket just jingle-jangling around. I only found out about flat-plates AFTER doing the build, otherwise I would have incorporated one.

An absolute monster. It doesn't have intergrated graphics but that is what my 4090 is for. It fixed every issue that I was having and it runs great. Other reviews say that it runs hot. I have just started using it but will make sure there is always lots of airflow to help keep it running as cool as can be.
To me, this is a great jump from my OCed i7 2600k cpu. I see a lot of potential for overclocking this thing for years to come. Hopefully I can get some good performance from this.

name: Intel Core i7-13700K 3.4 GHz 16-Core Processor
comments: Fast as HELL. Just make sure you are on the latest BIOS and not using MCE (multi-core enhancement), just to be safe for ultimate long-term reliability. Not like it needs it to be honest, as it is SO fast out of the box. Just unfortunate that it's not particularly safe to overclock it when the point of buying a "K" series is to overclock.
Amazing cpu stays cool and even able to play with a rtx 4090 pretty well in all games

The Central Processing Unit is the “brain” of the computer, a super-fast, streamlined filing system, or data handler, as Richard Feynman describes:
One of the miseries of life is that everybody names things a little bit wrong, and so it makes everything a little harder to understand in the world than it would be if it would be named differently. ¶ A computer does not primarily compute, in the sense of doing arithmetic. Strange. Although they call them computers, that’s not what they primarily do. They primarily are filing systems. ¶ People in the computer business say: “They’re not really computers, they’re DA-TA HAND-LERS.” Alright, that’s nice. Data handlers would have been a better name because it gives a better idea of the idea of a filing system where there’s a lot of data on cards and you handle it, you take cards out, look at them, put them back, and so on.
There’s an Intel Core i7-13700K 3.4 GHz 16-Core Processor in Interwebs Communotron 2023. It has worked without issues since building the machine in the end of 2023, so I’m satisfied.
fast and powerful, terrible to cool even with a loop but hey its not throttling
Perfect CPU for a gaming o prestational computer. It does its work but keep an eye on the temperatures.

Outstanding performance if you can get it for a good price. I got mine through a microcenter bundle and could not be happier with the choice. Upgrading from a 10700k, the difference is night and day.
I've personally never had any temp issues even with heavy gaming, but it definitely does get hot so be sure to pair with a well-equipped cooling solution.
Works great , great space heater

Found it to be a well-worth upgrade from my i5-9400f. Currently overclocking to where it consistently runs around 5.0Ghz and does not get hotter than 70 C while gaming or heavy loads and idles around 45-50 C (due to the Intel Turbo Boost)
Despite the well-publicized stability issues, this has been a fantastic CPU that's done everything I've asked of it.
Please don't melt yourself to death with your power limit issues.

name: AMD Ryzen 7 8700G 4.2 GHz 8-Core Processor
comments: Originally, I bought this to use as integrated graphics. However, I decided to splurge and get a GPU as well….ah well! Note: The included stock cooler is...fine. I chose to replace it with a larger ThermalRight cooler. If I were to do this again, I would have chosen a CPU without a cooler.

Overpriced? I feel so. The reason why I went with the 8700G was because it had integrated graphics and that's always handy in case your gpu craps the bed. Currently overclocked with Ryzen Master and before the GPU, I tested it out playing Helldivers 2 and it managed to get 60+ fps on medium settings. I was pretty impressed.
I had used i7-8809G and Ryzen 9 6900HX in the past, but the performance was not enough. I really like this CPU. The memory used is recommended to be DDR5-6000 or higher.

name: Intel Core i5-13600KF 3.5 GHz 14-Core Processor
comments: Perfect for a 4k gaming pc with good productivity performance. It draws a good amount of power but with a good cooler , everything is under control
Aside from needing to update the BIOS on my motherboard, there have been no issues with my CPU. Usage in game barely ever goes over 20%.

blasts basic programming tasks and doesn't get too hot.
i cannot complain.
Does everything I need it to.

Runs my FPS games at highest setting with 50% load on CPU. GPU is going to be the bottle neck with this champion of a CPU. It can run hot, but with my Corsair iCUE H115i ELITE CAPELLIX XT 89 CFM Liquid, it stays under 50 C.
Big help for editing videos and Adobe editing apps

insane how good this is for 175. like I mean I know all the noise happening with intel right now, but I still think this is the best CPU for the price at the time at least, like the only other CPU that can compete with this in the price point I purchased at was the 7600x and this was still 30 dollars cheaper, granted I don't have the upgradability but I like the efficiency of this chip because I'm not held back by only having 6-8 cores for my 3d rendering, cad, or editing programs. Overall, I'm extremely happy with my purchase I've had the chip for a little over a month now and I have literally zero complaints so far. Hopefully I have this for 5-6 years.
So far so good. Stable temperature and perfect for productivity.
Prime black Friday for 175. It's fast, should run 2k for a very long time and fingers crossed it won't detonate like the i7 and i9
Fast, stable, great price, and relatively easy to cool.

name: AMD Ryzen 5 5600GT 3.6 GHz 6-Core Processor
comments: Cpu runs great, the integrated graphics are amazing for what I play. (TF2 and Valorant) can keep a solid frame rate, and temps are great.
Ended up with one after ordering a Ryzen 5 5600G, no complaints so far, seems like the exact same product with maybe a tiny bit more performance.

name: Intel Core i9-14900KS 3.2 GHz 24-Core Processor
Intel Core i7-14700F 2.1 GHz 20-Core Processor
comments: It's been holding be out really well, and I've checked out All the specs, really good for its price.
